Just large enough for Dwight to push his arm through. David flinched as fingers found his, wrapping around the hand still braced against the weight. “You’re doing good,” Dwight said gently, voice tight but even. “Just keep talking to me. We’ve got you. You’re gonna be okay.” David clenched his jaw, willing himself not to panic. He focused on the contact. Not the dust. Not the stone. Not the crush of air that wouldn’t come back in. It wasn’t much. But it was the closest to outside he’d been in over an hour. “You better be right,” he rasped. “Don’t suppose you found a crowbar down here with me?” That got a light chuckle from Dwight, the soft sound easing back some of the anxiety. This was good. They had opened up some space. Let in some light. Just that much closer to getting back into the open air again. He could handle this. It was hardly the worst trial he had gone through, anyways. “Alright,” Felix called. “Top layer’s mostly clear on this side. I can see the shape of him — his shoulder’s wedged under that flat slab. If we shift it straight up and back—” CRACK. It wasn’t a collapse. Just a single, fist-sized chunk of sandstone coming loose from somewhere higher up. But it landed square on the pile, driving a lower stone into David’s hip like a hammer. He jerked — instinctive, immediate — and the pile answered . The weight on his chest dropped half an inch, his body compressing under it like a sponge. Dust billowed into his mouth. The stone above his head scraped down hard against his forearm, and the muscles screamed — finally reaching their limit after holding for far too long. And somewhere deep inside... something snapped . He gasped — a full breath for the first time in minutes — and the sudden expansion made everything shift again. He shoved hard against the nearest stone, pressing his shoulder against it, kicking down to try and twist his hip away from the pressure. It wasn’t a choice, but pure reflex. He couldn’t help it. His body demanded oxygen. Demanded motion. Demanded freedom . “David — stop ! You’re making it worse!” Felix’s voice cracked as stone shifted overhead. But David wasn’t listening. He was gone. Every muscle seized in panic, heaving against the crush, desperate to escape. His thoughts blurred into static, a single command screaming louder than pain, louder than logic: OUT . His left arm tore free of its space, elbow crashing the side of the pile as he tried to lever his torso upward — sheer instinct, blind and useless. The stone he’d been holding off finally dropped, slamming down against his forehead with a brutal scrape, narrowly missing his eye. The shift collapsed the fragile gap Dwight had carved out. The moment he felt the rush of air vanish, Dwight yanked his arm back with a sharp yell, stone rasping down his forearm and tearing a line through both skin and jacket in a single clean snag. He stumbled back hard, clutching his wrist. “He’s panicking!” “David, stop ! You have to calm down!” Felix snapped, already scrambling to find a grip on the nearest rock. “You’re going to bring it all down!” David was beyond listening, the insistent cries of his teammates drowned out by the screaming in his own mind. He thrashed — not in any useful direction, not toward rescue — just against everything . His limbs struck out at pressure points, searching for a weakness in the crush, but found only more stone. He wasn’t fighting them. He was fighting everything . The dust clawing down his throat. The weight grinding in around his ribs. The dark. The silence. The sheer wrongness of his body being unable to move, to breathe, to be . Cause and effect had left the building. Reason was gone. There was only movement now — fast, feral, unthinking. A primal spasm that flung his hips sideways, body twisting toward a space that didn’t exist, trying to be elsewhere by sheer force alone. Above him, Felix barely caught a loose chunk before it tumbled. He flung it away, hand already grabbing at another. “He’s going to destabilize everything,” he snapped. “Help me get this clear!” Dwight scrambled back to the pile, skidding on grit, blood streaking down his arm. “David, please—!” For a moment, it looked like he might actually get free. David’s shoulder shoved upward, scraping stone aside with a jagged screech. One slab near his head slipped loose, dragging a pale gouge in the rock as it rolled — and a gap opened. Light. Air. But then gravity remembered him again. The rubble poured down, sweeping across the pile from the remains of the staircase above. A chunk near the top shifted, dislodging the stone above his left arm. It dropped — hard — pinning him sideways and dragging his arm down with it. Grit sprayed out in all directions as the weight surged. The weight dropped, slow but unrelenting, filling every open space. The weight crushed inward, and David’s chest folded beneath it. His ribs compressed, oxygen stolen before he could even try to reclaim it. His vision exploded into white — too tight, too loud, too much — and the world tipped sideways into silence. “Felix, the center’s falling!” Dwight shouted. “I see it — brace that corner — shit — David! ” Another stone went flying as Dwight tore at the edge of the collapse. Dust plumed up, stinging his eyes. “David?! David, are you okay?” Felix stepped hesitantly back from the rubble.
